title: FAA still probing whether SMART AI tool played a role in the nationwide ground stop
subtitle: Secretary Duffy says the SMART air-traffic AI, expanded nationwide three days earlier, played no role in the November 13 outage — but officials have not cleared it and the investigation into the "router flooding" trigger is ongoing.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Three days after the FAA's nationwide ground stop on November 13, officials are still investigating whether the agency's new AI air-traffic tool, SMART — Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories — contributed to the outage. The stop ran roughly from 4 p.m. to 8:15 p.m. ET and resulted in more than 12,462 flight cancellations on Friday and 3,400 on Saturday morning. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has attributed the trigger to a router installed during a switch that "started flooding other routers in our air traffic control system". He says SMART, which went live across all 22 air route traffic control centers on November 10, played no role. Senator Markwayne Mullin, speaking on the investigation, declined to clear it: "You can't rule out anything."

The scrutiny matters because of the timing. The SMART expansion to the full network happened three days before the outage. The FAA has emphasised that SMART "cannot be used to replace the critical role air traffic controllers play", and that the system was designed as decision support, not control. A congressional letter earlier this year had warned about AI's "potential to interfere with decision-making by experienced air traffic controllers or to hallucinate safety-critical information". Duffy has asked Congress for $50 billion to upgrade the broader air traffic control system.

This is the first U.S. federal-infrastructure incident in which an AI decision-support system was installed, then correlated in time with a nationwide failure, then investigated as a possible contributing factor. Even if SMART is formally cleared, the investigation itself will set the template for how AI tools get deployed into safety-critical national systems — rollout cadence, change-control, how post-incident review handles AI components whose behavior is not fully specified.

A note for learners: when AI is added to a safety-critical system, the hard problem isn't whether the model is accurate. It's whether the surrounding change-control process can tell you, after an incident, whether the model contributed. If the audit trail for AI decisions isn't as good as the one for routers and routing tables, you can't actually rule the model in or out — which is a different kind of failure than a bug.
